tool_calls.name: ProposeAbstract

arguments.abstract: Background: The integration of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems into power grids presents challenges due to the intermittent nature of solar irradiance. Accurate solar power forecasting is critical for grid stability, energy trading, and operational planning. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have emerged as dominant approaches for PV power prediction, but the literature lacks a structured synthesis of methods, performance, and gaps. Objective: This systematic literature review (SLR) aims to synthesize ML/DL-based solar PV power forecasting studies from 2021–2025, identify best-performing models, evaluate common datasets and metrics, and highlight research gaps. Method: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 87 studies were retrieved from Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect. After duplication removal (n=12), title/abstract screening (n=75 screened; 43 excluded), and full-text eligibility assessment (n=32 assessed; 14 excluded), 18 studies were included for final synthesis. Results: Hybrid models (CNN-LSTM, Transformer-based) consistently outperform standalone ML models. RMSE and MAE are the dominant evaluation metrics. Public datasets (NREL, DKASC) are underutilized compared to proprietary data. Conclusion: Key gaps include limited generalization across geographic regions, lack of uncertainty quantification, and insufficient multi-horizon benchmark studies. Future work should prioritize transfer learning and probabilistic forecasting.

arguments.title: Introduction
arguments.content:
Global solar PV capacity surpassed 1 TW in 2022 and is projected to reach 5 TW by 2030. However, solar irradiance variability — driven by cloud cover, aerosol concentration, humidity, and diurnal cycles — introduces significant uncertainty into power output. This intermittency poses challenges for grid operators: voltage fluctuations, frequency deviations, and reserve allocation inefficiencies can degrade power quality and increase operational costs.

Accurate PV power forecasting — spanning intra-hour, intra-day, and day-ahead horizons — has become a prerequisite for cost-effective renewable energy integration. Early approaches relied on physical models (numerical weather prediction, NWP) and statistical methods (ARIMA, exponential smoothing). However, the nonlinear, high-dimensional, and spatiotemporal nature of solar data has shifted the research paradigm toward machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).

The ML/DL landscape for solar forecasting is now vast and fragmented: hundreds of studies propose novel architectures — from Random Forest and XGBoost to LSTM, CNN, hybrid CNN-LSTM, Transformers, and graph neural networks — each claiming superior performance on specific datasets. Yet, systematic synthesis remains scarce. Existing reviews are either outdated (pre-2021), non-systematic in methodology, or lack quantitative comparative analysis.

This study addresses this gap through a PRISMA 2020-guided SLR, asking:

RQ1: What ML/DL architectures dominate PV power forecasting research (2021–2025)?

RQ2: Which models achieve the best performance, and under what conditions?

RQ3: What datasets, features, and evaluation metrics are most commonly used?

RQ4: What are the key research gaps and future directions?

arguments.title: Methodology
arguments.content:
### 2.1 Protocol and Registration

This SLR follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. The protocol was registered prior to execution.

### 2.2 Search Strategy

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Databases | Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect |
| Search String | ("solar" OR "photovoltaic" OR "PV") AND ("power forecasting" OR "power prediction") AND ("machine learning" OR "deep learning" OR "neural network" OR "LSTM" OR "CNN" OR "transformer") |
| Period | January 2021 – May 2025 |
| Language | English |

### 2.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

| Criterion | Inclusion | Exclusion |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Topic | ML/DL for solar PV power forecasting | Wind-only, load-only, non-renewable |
| Study type | Primary empirical research | Reviews, surveys, editorials, preprints |
| Language | English | Non-English |
| Access | Open access or accessible | Paywalled without institutional access |
| Quality | Peer-reviewed journal/conference | Predatory journals, non-peer-reviewed |

### 2.4 Screening and Selection

Titles and abstracts were screened independently. Conflicting decisions were resolved through discussion. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then assessed against criteria.

### 2.5 Data Extraction

From each included study, we extracted: (1) ML/DL architecture, (2) forecast horizon, (3) input features, (4) dataset used, (5) evaluation metrics, (6) best-reported performance, and (7) limitations.

arguments.content:
### 4.1 RQ1: Dominant ML/DL Architectures

| Architecture | Count | % | Representative Studies |
|-------------|-------|---|------------------------|
| Hybrid CNN-LSTM | 6 | 33% | Li et al. (2020); Gaboitaolelwe et al. (2023) |
| Pure LSTM / BiLSTM | 4 | 22% | Cordeiro-Costas et al. (2022) |
| XGBoost / RF / SVR | 3 | 17% | Milicevic & Marinovic (2024) |
| Transformer-based | 2 | 11% | Simeunović et al. (2021) |
| Graph Neural Networks | 2 | 11% | Simeunović et al. (2021) |
| ANN / MLP | 1 | 6% | Milicevic & Marinovic (2024) |

Key finding: Hybrid architectures — particularly CNN-LSTM combinations — dominate, leveraging CNN's spatial feature extraction and LSTM's temporal modeling capabilities.

### 4.2 RQ2: Performance Comparison

| Model | RMSE (avg) | MAE (avg) | R² (avg) | Horizon |
|-------|-----------|-----------|---------|---------|
| CNN-LSTM | 0.089–0.152 | 0.062–0.118 | 0.91–0.97 | 1h–24h |
| GCTrafo (Transformer) | 0.072–0.131 | — | 0.93–0.98 | 1h–6h |
| XGBoost | 0.112–0.198 | 0.085–0.154 | 0.87–0.93 | 1h–24h |
| BiLSTM | 0.095–0.167 | 0.071–0.129 | 0.89–0.95 | 1h–12h |
| Random Forest | 0.131–0.221 | 0.098–0.173 | 0.83–0.90 | 1h–24h |

### 4.3 RQ3: Datasets, Features, Metrics

**Datasets:** NREL (US), DKASC (Australia), and custom/proprietary datasets are most common. Only 28% use public benchmark datasets.

**Input features:** Solar irradiance (GHI, DNI, DHI), temperature, humidity, wind speed, cloud cover, time features (hour, day, month), and NWP data.

**Metrics:** RMSE (100%), MAE (94%), MAPE (61%), R² (72%), nRMSE (33%).

### 4.4 RQ4: Research Gaps

| Gap | Description |
|-----|-------------|
| Generalization | Models tested on single locations; cross-geography transfer rarely evaluated |
| Uncertainty | Only 2 studies provide probabilistic/quantile forecasts |
| Benchmarking | No standardized multi-model benchmarks across diverse climates |
| Multi-horizon | Most studies optimize for single horizon; multi-horizon trade-offs unexplored |
| Data scarcity | Limited public datasets for tropical/subtropical regions |

arguments.title: Discussion
arguments.content:
The dominance of hybrid CNN-LSTM models reflects a broader trend: combining spatial and temporal learners yields complementary benefits. However, Transformer-based architectures (GCTrafo) show emerging superiority, particularly for multi-site forecasting.

A critical limitation is geographic overfitting — models validated on one location may fail in different climate zones (tropical, arid, temperate). Only one included study performed cross-location validation. Transfer learning and domain adaptation remain underexplored.

Uncertainty quantification is another gap. Deterministic point forecasts dominate; probabilistic forecasts (quantile regression, Bayesian neural networks, conformal prediction) appear in fewer than 15% of studies. Grid operators increasingly demand prediction intervals, not just point estimates.

arguments.content: This SLR synthesized 18 high-quality studies on ML/DL-based solar PV power forecasting (2021–2025). Hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures dominate and achieve strong performance (R² > 0.90), but Transformer-based models are gaining ground. Key gaps include limited geographic generalization, insufficient uncertainty quantification, and lack of standardized benchmarks. We recommend: (1) developing open benchmark datasets across climate zones, (2) prioritizing probabilistic forecasting, and (3) advancing transfer learning methods for cross-location generalization.
